name: S. M. Street (Mittayi Theruvu)
tagline: Kozhikode’s sweet‑meat lane and street‑food heart in the cool season
summary: Historic Mittayi Theruvu (S. M. Street) is Kozhikode’s compact food and shopping circuit — famous for Kozhikodan halwa, banana chips, bakeries and old tea‑shops; best explored in the cool season…
description: S. M. Street, locally Mittayi Theruvu or Sweet‑meat Street, sits in central Kozhikode and has been a commercial and culinary hub since the Zamorin era. The lane still shows the city’s merchant mix: halwa counters, banana‑chip sellers, bakeries, spice and textile stalls and a small Parsi fire temple.

For food visitors the street offers quick, take‑away classics (halwa cut by weight, banana chips, sweet and savoury snacks) and access to nearby Mappila and beach stalls that complete a Malabar food walk. The lane’s compact scale makes it ideal for a morning or evening walk, sampling small portions and buying gifts to carry home.

The street matters culturally as well as culinarily: it inspired literature, carries old shopfronts and the granite statue of S. K. Pottekkatt, and is a living example of Kozhikode’s layered trade and food history. Confirm opening times and stall availability before you travel, especially around festivals and Ramadan when routines change.
highlights: Kozhikodan halwa counters — halwa is sold and weighed by the piece
Banana chips and fried snacks in coconut oil
Small, historic bakeries and tea‑shop breakfasts (pathiri, puttu)
Parsi fire temple and the S. K. Pottekkatt statue — literary link
Easy one‑to‑two hour walking food circuit linking Mananchira and nearby beach stalls

sections.heading: Background
body: The lane’s Malayalam name, Mittayi Theruvu, means ‘sweets street’ and traces to Gujarati and other merchant communities invited to Calicut in the Zamorin period. Over time the street became known for halwa and snacks stacked in glossy slabs and trays.

A focused renovation and beautification (overhead lines removed, lamp posts and pedestrian works) in recent years made the lane more pedestrian friendly while preserving its market character; the street remains a working market with old family shops alongside newer cafés.

sections.heading: What to see and do
body: Start in the morning for halwa tasting — ask for small quantities and buy by weight so you can try two or three flavours. Pair halwa with banana chips or a tea‑shop snack such as puttu or pathiri in nearby Kuttichira.

Look for the Parsi fire temple, the Pottekkatt statue, and the old bakeries where traditional snacks are still made. Use the lane as the food stage of a larger Malabar circuit: halwa at SM Street, biryani on Kannur Road, then evening beach stalls for fried fish and pazham pori.

sections.heading: Plan your visit
body: Go early (morning) to beat the crowds and heat — halwa counters are easiest to browse then. The street is compact (about 1–2 km of market and lanes); allow 1–2 hours for a relaxed food walk with tasting stops.

Keep small change, buy halwa in small packets, ask about shelf life if you are travelling, and watch for festival or Ramadan‑time changes to opening patterns. Confirm large‑group arrangements or tour needs with local DTPC if required.

latest.text: Updated travel guides note the street remains a pedestrian‑friendly market after previous beautification works and recommend morning visits for halwa and a calmer experience.

visitorInfo.bestTime: Cool, dry season — roughly November to May; mornings are best for halwa counters.
visitorInfo.howToReach: About 500 m walk from Kozhikode Railway Station; Calicut International Airport (CCJ) is roughly 22 km. The lane sits beside Mananchira — reach by taxi, auto or a short walk from central Kozhikode.
etiquette: Visit early morning to avoid crowds and try halwa when counters are easiest to browse.
Buy halwa by weight (ask for small quantities of different flavours) and carry small notes for quick transactions.
Keep valuables close; the street is busy and seating is limited — plan a cafe break nearby.
If you travel during Ramadan or local festivals, expect altered opening times and extra evening stalls.
